Chapter 3: The Power of Owning Our Stories
So, you’ve taken a look at your story—really examined it. But now comes the next big step: actually owning what you’ve found. And honestly, this is where a lot of us get stuck. It’s tempting to distance ourselves from the messy parts of our lives, right? But real resilience doesn’t come from hiding or pretending things didn’t happen. It grows when we’re brave enough to face our struggles head-on and embrace every part of them.
Think about this: there was a woman who, after a tough breakup, just wanted to erase the entire past year. She avoided seeing mutual friends, deleted every photo, and tried to move on as quickly as possible. But the pain? It kept showing up—often when she least expected it. Healing didn’t really start until she let herself feel the full weight of her hurt, and admitted the part she played in how things ended. That’s when things began to shift.
Owning your story means accepting all of it—the wins and the mistakes, the proud moments and the ones you wish you could take back. It’s recognizing that, yes, your experiences shape you, but they don’t have to define you. A lot of people worry that admitting their flaws or missteps will just open the door to judgment or rejection. But here’s the truth: it’s actually this kind of honesty that brings us closer together and helps us grow.
I want you to picture a leader who, after making a public mistake, chooses to stand in front of her team and own up to it. You can imagine the tension in the room. But as she speaks openly about what happened and what she’s learned from it, something changes. Her openness encourages others to share their own struggles, and suddenly, there’s a real sense of trust and accountability in the room.
Too often, we fall into the trap of hiding parts of our story—thinking only the polished, picture-perfect version is worth sharing. But that kind of perfectionism? It just makes us feel alone. It pushes us away from others, and even from ourselves. When we finally decide to own the whole story—the real, messy, human story—we open up space for empathy, creativity, and connection.
Take, for example, a parent who feels guilty after snapping in anger at his child. Instead of brushing it off, he chooses to apologize. Sure, it’s awkward at first, but it lets them both connect on a deeper level. And when the child sees a parent willing to take responsibility, she feels safe enough to share her own feelings, too.
The act of owning your story is pure courage. It means facing some uncomfortable truths and letting go of the need for constant approval. It’s about stepping into the arena—vulnerable, yes, but also open to growth, connection, and change.
This isn’t about blaming yourself or getting stuck on the mistakes you’ve made. It’s about learning from your experiences and carrying those lessons forward. Every time you own a part of your story, the grip of shame loosens, and your ability to bounce back gets stronger.
Like the friend who, after years of hiding her anxiety, finally shares her story with a close group. Instead of judgment, she’s met with support and understanding. By owning her experience, she actually gives others the courage to do the same.
That’s the real power of owning your story. It’s what transforms struggle into strength. It deepens your self-awareness, builds empathy, and becomes the foundation for rising strong. In a world that’s always chasing perfection, choosing to embrace your full, unfiltered story? That’s nothing short of revolutionary.
